Three Card Poker Basics: Ante, Pair Plus, and the House Edge

Published September 11, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Three Card Poker gets pitched to new players as "the fast, simple one" — a single three-card hand, one decision, no waiting on a multi-street betting round. That reputation is fair as far as it goes, but the game actually runs two separate bets with two separate house edges bundled under one table, and treating them as a single decision is where a lot of players quietly give up more than they need to.

How a hand actually plays out

Each player places an Ante bet, and optionally a Pair Plus bet, before any cards are dealt. Every player and the dealer then receive three cards, face down. After looking at their hand, each player decides either to fold, forfeiting the Ante, or to make a Play bet equal to the Ante, staying in the hand. The dealer then reveals their own three cards; if the dealer doesn't qualify (most commonly requiring at least a queen-high hand), Ante bets pay even money automatically and the Play bet pushes. If the dealer does qualify, both the Ante and Play bets are compared against the dealer's hand independently and settled at even money based on who has the better three-card hand.

That's the entire structure of the base game — one decision (play or fold), resolved against a dealer hand that either qualifies or doesn't. There's no drawing, no additional cards, and no strategy decisions once the play/fold call is made.

Hand rankings: why three cards flip the usual order

Because a three-card hand has fewer possible combinations than a five-card hand, the relative rarity of certain hands changes, which reorders the hand ranking compared to standard poker. In Three Card Poker, a straight is rarer than a flush, so straights outrank flushes — the opposite of five-card poker hand rankings. From highest to lowest, the order runs: straight flush, three of a kind, straight, flush, pair, high card. It's a small detail, but it trips up players who assume poker hand rankings are universal across every poker-adjacent table game.

Worth remembering: a straight beats a flush in Three Card Poker specifically because there are fewer possible three-card straights than three-card flushes — the math behind the game reorders the hands, not just the house's house rules.

The Ante/Play decision and the Q-6-4 rule

The only real strategic decision in Three Card Poker is whether to make the Play bet or fold after seeing your hand, and it has a clean, well-established correct answer: play any hand of Queen-6-4 or better, and fold anything weaker. This single rule — commonly shortened to the "Q-6-4 rule" — is mathematically optimal and isn't a rough approximation; it's the exact break-even threshold given the dealer's qualifying requirement and the game's payout structure. Playing worse hands than Q-6-4 loses value on average, and folding better hands gives up value the odds say you're entitled to.

Correct Ante/Play strategy alone gets the base game's house edge down to roughly 3.4%, which is higher than blackjack played with correct basic strategy but still a manageable, well-understood number — and dramatically better than playing by feel, since deviating from Q-6-4 in either direction (folding too much or playing too many weak hands) measurably increases the house's edge over time.

The Ante Bonus: a side payout on the main bet

Many tables layer an Ante Bonus onto the Ante wager itself — an additional payout, independent of whether the hand beats the dealer, triggered purely by the strength of the player's own hand. A straight typically pays a small bonus, three of a kind pays considerably more, and a straight flush pays the largest bonus of all, often regardless of whether the dealer's hand ultimately beats the player's. Because it pays out on hand strength alone, the Ante Bonus is one of the more overlooked value boosts in the game — it applies automatically to any qualifying Ante bet, with no separate wager or decision required, which makes it different from Pair Plus in an important way.

Pair Plus: a completely separate bet

Pair Plus is an optional side bet, made instead of or alongside the Ante, that pays out purely based on the player's own three-card hand — a pair or better — with no comparison to the dealer's hand at all. Because it never interacts with the dealer's cards, Pair Plus can win even on a hand the player would otherwise fold, and it can lose even on a hand strong enough to beat the dealer. The two bets are fully independent systems running on the same three cards.

Pair Plus pay tables vary meaningfully by casino — some pay a flat rate on any pair and scale up through straight, flush, three of a kind, and straight flush, while others use a steeper or flatter curve. That variation matters more than it looks: a pay table that pays less generously on a pair (the most common winning hand by a wide margin) carries a noticeably higher house edge than one that's more generous at the bottom of the payout scale, even if the two tables look similar at a glance for the rare top-end hands.

Ante/Play (base game)Pair Plus (side bet)
Compared against dealer?YesNo — judged on its own
Strategy involved?Yes — the Q-6-4 ruleNone; it's a fixed wager
Typical house edge~3.4% with correct playVaries by pay table, often 2%-7%+
Can win while the other loses?Yes — fully independent outcomesYes — fully independent outcomes

Comparing the two bets side by side

Because Pair Plus's house edge depends heavily on the specific pay table posted at that table — something that varies by casino and even by table within the same casino — it's genuinely worth checking the payout card before sitting down if minimizing house edge matters to you. A generous Pair Plus pay table can approach the Ante/Play bet's edge; a stingy one can run considerably worse. The Ante/Play bet, by contrast, has a fixed, well-documented house edge as long as Q-6-4 strategy is followed, since it's set by the game's core rules rather than by a variable payout table.

This is a useful habit to carry into other table games too — see our piece on blackjack side bets and why they carry a higher house edge for the same underlying idea applied to a different game: side bets that pay out on hand strength alone, independent of the main game's outcome, tend to have both higher variance and a wider range of possible house edges depending on the specific pay table in front of you.

Common mistakes at the table

The most common mistake is folding hands that meet or beat Q-6-4 out of caution, especially borderline hands like Q-6-4 itself or Q-7-2, which feel weak but are mathematically correct plays. The second is treating Pair Plus as "part of" the main bet rather than a fully separate wager with its own edge — players sometimes assume a strong Ante/Play result means Pair Plus paid off too, when the two are unrelated outside of sharing the same three cards. The third is sitting down without a glance at the Pair Plus pay table, which can mean unknowingly playing a version of the side bet with a meaningfully worse house edge than the table next to it.

Frequently asked questions

What's the single most important strategy rule in Three Card Poker?

Play any hand of Queen-6-4 or better, and fold anything weaker. This is mathematically optimal and gets the base game's house edge to roughly 3.4%.

Is Pair Plus a good bet?

It depends entirely on the specific pay table at that casino. A generous pay table can be competitive with the Ante/Play bet's edge; a stingy one, especially on the pair payout, can run considerably worse. Check the posted payout card before betting it.

Why does a straight beat a flush in this game?

With only three cards in play, there are fewer possible straights than possible flushes, which makes a straight the rarer — and therefore higher-ranked — hand, reversing the usual five-card poker order.

Can I win the hand against the dealer but still lose my Pair Plus bet?

Yes. Pair Plus is judged entirely on your own hand strength and never compares to the dealer's cards, so the two bets can — and often do — produce different results on the same three cards.
